The prospect of tighter monetary policy kept Treasury yields elevated, with 10-year borrowing costs poised to match a 2007 run of 29 closes above 5% in the same year.

Globally, investors are betting that major central banks, including the Fed, European Central Bank and Bank of England, will keep rates largely unchanged for years once they have finished hiking at the end of 2027.

Higher interest rates and yields are typically negative for gold, which doesn’t pay interest. A gauge of the dollar has also risen 0.5% this week, making bullion priced in the US currency more expensive for most buyers.

Gold is “now firmly in an air pocket, with very little technical support until the US$3,300 and US$3,400 region”, said Justin Lin, a strategist at Global X ETFs. The metal “looks very fragile now, and I struggle to see what could turn momentum around just yet”.

Bullion has fallen by about a third since the US-Iran war began in late February, as higher energy costs fuelled inflation. The precious metal has also been caught up in a rout in technology stocks, with Asian equities tracking a decline on Wall Street driven by concerns around the AI trade.

Spot gold fell 2% to US$3,552.06 an ounce at 3.10pm Singapore time. Silver dropped 2.5% to US$41.88 an ounce, after sinking nearly 5% in the previous session. Platinum and palladium also declined. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Apple working on AI agent for device control, apps, browsing and coding
data.description:
Apple is developing its own autonomous artificial intelligence agent that can get things done on behalf of users, looking to enter a fast-growing market already being pursued by OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta Platforms and others.

The company outlined the plans in job listings added to its website this week. In one listing, Apple said it is seeking a senior engineering manager for a proactive, agentic AI assistant. The system will write code, browse the web, control apps and navigate devices on a user’s behalf, according to the post.

The move follows the breakout success of Meta’s Muse, which has captured the attention of consumers in recent months with its ability to make restaurant reservations, book travel arrangements and prepare news briefings. There has also been a proliferation of tools that let AI control Mac computers and program software. 

Shares of Meta and Anthropic slid in late trading after Bloomberg News reported on Apple’s efforts. Meta fell nearly 2%, while Anthropic dropped more than 3%. 

Anthropic recently widened user testing of its own agent, called Duet, while OpenAI has expanded the capabilities of Dots. And Alphabet Inc’s Google overhauled its agent, now called Tasks, earlier this week. Like Elon Musk’s Grok Bot, Tasks lets the system make phone calls on a user’s behalf – in addition to offering standard AI agent features.

Apple’s App Store has been dominated by AI agents, with Muse long occupying the No. 2 spot among free apps, just behind TikTok, on Nov 19. OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude were also in the top five.

OpenAI, Anthropic and Musk’s SpaceXSI are also behind popular developer coding tools Codex, Claude Code and Cursor.

Bloomberg News reported earlier in November that Apple was developing its own AI agent offering, but the new job listings offer fresh evidence of the company’s plans. Apple has eyed introducing the service as soon as end-2027, but development remains in the early stages. An Apple spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment.

“Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does,” the job listing reads. “It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple.”

The listing says the company has a team building the “foundation for that future” and that Apple is looking for the hired manager to “make it real”. John Ternus, the tech giant’s new chief executive officer, has been pushing software engineering chief Craig Federighi to move faster and take a bolder approach to AI – with an agent being key to that effort.

“People already do their most valuable work by moving fluidly between tools: a browser, a document, a terminal, an editor, a service. We’re building AI agents that can do the same,” the listing says. The posting adds that Apple is working on agents that can “plan and carry out multi-step tasks” across apps, browsers, command lines, code and application programming interfaces, and they can “coordinate specialised subagents along the way”.

The company strongly indicates its platform would be capable of autonomously navigating the interfaces of its operating systems. The listing specifically mentions development of “general-purpose computer-use agents”, the technology that allows ChatGPT and Muse to control a Mac. Google Gemini added such functionality earlier on Nov 19.

Another central component is privacy, with Apple saying that safety needs to be built into the system’s design. “Agents that can run code, use credentials and act on a user’s behalf need strong permission models, sandboxing and transparency.”

Sandboxing is a process that lets engineers test software without the risk of it breaking out into external networks, the rest of the operating system or the broader internet.

As the company develops its own agent, Apple is also making it more difficult for competing bots to gain broad control over its computers. In the beta version of the upcoming macOS 27.3 operating system, it has introduced new warning screens that prompt users to reconsider granting third-party agents permission to control their Macs.

With the change in 27.3, ChatGPT users now need to engage in 14 distinct steps to enable support for third-party computer-use tools, up from four. While Apple has positioned the shift as a move to protect customers, some AI companies and users see it as an attempt to slow down the competition. 

Apple has already been sued by the US Justice Department for actions such as blocking third-party access to features and hardware.

While Apple is still far from introducing its own full-fledged AI agent, it has taken steps to integrate its Siri digital assistant more deeply into third-party apps. The upcoming iOS 27.3 release lays the groundwork for deeper collaboration between Siri AI and outside applications, allowing the assistant to, say, book a car or restaurant reservation.

Still, the updated system doesn’t go as far as a full-fledged agent, which can autonomously carry out complex tasks across multiple apps and services in the background with little additional instruction from the user. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Wall St ends sharply lower on AI selloff, S&P 500, Dow in correction
data.description:
NEW YORK - US stocks extended their rout on Nov 20, and the S&P 500 and the Dow both confirmed corrections after Anthropic’s momentous debut fell flat, exacerbating worries about the AI trade that has driven this year’s stock market rally.

All three major US equity indexes ended sharply lower.

The Dow and the S&P 500 are now more than 10% below their record closing highs,confirming both indexes have entered a correction.

The bellwether S&P 500 notched its seventh consecutive drop, its longest losing streak since February 2020.

The S&P 500 and the Dowlogged their largest weekly percentage losses since April 2025, when US President Donald Trump announced his market-rattling “liberation day” tariff package.

The Nasdaq’s weekly drop was its largest since March 2020. The tech-heavy index has dipped into negative territory for the year.

“This is clearly a challenging day for capital markets, and as we head into a Friday close, appears to be accelerating to a certain degree,” said Bill Northey, senior investment director at US Bank Wealth Management in Billings, Montana.

“But as we step back and evaluate fundamentals and sentiment, sentiment is clearly winning the day today.”

“Sentiment is always the more powerful force in the immediate space, whereas fundamentals tend to win out over time,” Northey added, referring to economic strength and solid corporate earnings, among other things.

Anthropic’s supersized debut as a publicly held company, which was intended to raise as much as US$2 trillion (S$2.5 trillion) in market cap, failed to catch fire on Nov 19, closing 17.1% above its US$83 offer price as enthusiasm for the stock faded throughout the session.

In its second day as a publicly held company, Anthropic’s shares fell 9.1%. Nvidia’s shares tumbled 13.8%.

The Anthropic IPO, combined with Nvidia’s quarterly earnings report, failed to dispel fears over risks associated with artificial intelligence and the massive expenditures on the nascent technology.

“Nvidia reported what might have been one of the greatest quarters in corporate earnings history; they did everything right,” said Chuck Carlson, chief executive officer at Horizon Investment Services in Hammond, Indiana. “A lot of people, myself included, were looking to the Anthropic debut to some extent as a clearing event, and it wasn’t.”

The Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index, which has powered much of the broader stock market’s gains in recent months, was up as much as 106.6% in mid-June. That lustre has faded, with the index’s year-to-date advance having shrunk to 18.7%.

Among hyperscalers, Amazon fell 3.9%, while Meta dropped 5.9%.

Neocloud firm CoreWeave fell 12.1% and its peer Nebius slid 16.1%.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 949.73 points, or 1.93%, to 48,147.33, the S&P 500 lost 265.41 points, or 3.70%, to 6,910.42 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 1,261.47 points, or 5.28%, to 22,617.73.

The CBOE Market Volatility Index, often referred to as Wall Street’s “fear gauge,” rose to its highest close since April 7, 2025.

Inflation, US Fed in focus

Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook said the central bank’s policy rate is not high enough to deal with inflation levels.

Markets are pricing a near-certain likelihood of a 25-basis-point interest rate hike at the Fed’s next meeting in December, according to CME Group’s FedWatch tool.

Next week’s personal consumption expenditures (PCE) figures will provide further clarity on the Fed’s monetary policy path after a hotter-than-expected October inflation report last week.

Among other movers, Intuit shares fell 12.8% after the company cut its annual revenue growth forecast and agreed to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for about US$3.68 billion, five years after acquiring it for nearly three times as much.

UnitedHealth rose 2.8% after TD Cowen upgraded its shares to a “buy” from a “hold” rating.

The AI selloff also sent Caterpillar 5% lower on worries over weakening demand for its power-generating and backup power equipment.

Cryptocurrency firms including Coinbase, Strategy and Robinhood tumbled between 6.3% and 9.6% after bitcoin dropped below the $60,000 level.

Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 3.77-to-1 ratio on the NYSE. There were 38 new highs and 1,199 new lows on the NYSE.

On the Nasdaq, 928 stocks rose and 3,964 fell as declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 4.27-to-1 ratio.

The S&P 500 posted 3 new 52-week highs and 28 new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 21 new highs and 826 new lows.

Volume on US exchanges was 25.19 billion shares, compared with the 19.50 billion average for the full session over the last 20 trading days. REUTERS

data.title: Anthropic pulls off mega IPO amid AI slump, gold tumbles: Markets this week
data.description:
SINGAPORE – Artificial intelligence company Anthropic pulled off a blockbuster stock market debut even as a sell-off in technology shares weighed on broader markets, while gold prices slumped as investors assessed the outlook for US interest rates.

Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, raised more than US$81 billion (S$105 billion) on Nov 19 in the biggest initial public offering (IPO) in history, topping SpaceX’s US$75 billion base deal. Its shares closed at US$97.17, more than 17% above its offer price.

Still, the historic debut did little to lift sentiment in the broader AI sector, with technology stocks continuing to face selling pressure over concerns about valuations and the significant sums being poured into AI development.

Shares of chip giant Nvidia fell 3.3% on Nov 19, extending their losing streak to six sessions, while Micron Technology declined 2.1%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell 2.25%, while the S&P 500 dipped 2.02%.

Zavier Wong, market analyst at eToro, said the broader market was grappling with several developments at once, including expectations of further US interest rate hikes, scrutiny over chip exports and a short-selling report targeting chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices.

He noted that Nvidia had also given up the gains it made following its latest earnings announcement, while the departure of its former chief executive Jensen Huang added to market uncertainty.

The chipmaker had reported a 103% year-on-year jump in revenue to US$115.8 billion for its third quarter ended Oct 25, beating analysts’ expectations. Its net profit more than doubled to US$65.3 billion, while revenue from its data centre business rose 110% to US$107.6 billion.

“The different factors are why the sell-off has been so hard to quell,” said Wong, noting that the S&P 500 had fallen for six consecutive sessions and was down about 8% from its record high in October.

“An interest rate hike in December is more or less priced in, which makes the Fed’s upcoming meeting the next key date the market is watching.”

Meanwhile, gold saw its worst weekly decline since March, tumbling about 7% to hover just above US$3,500 as expectations of further rate hikes and selling by investors seeking to cover losses in equities weighed on the precious metal.

Gold is down 8.5% in 2026 and is 37% below January’s intraday peak of US$5,602.

CMC Markets sales trader Alex Ho noted that the yield on the benchmark 10-year US Treasury note had risen above 5%, while real yields, which are adjusted for inflation, had climbed from 2.66% to 2.88% since Nov 9.

This has made gold, which does not pay interest, less attractive to investors. The AI stock sell-off also added to the pressure on the precious metal.

“When portfolios are hurting, investors sell what they can, not what they want... So gold is being sold to raise cash, but that is not the same as it failing as a hedge,” said Ho.

“A quick bounce is possible, but a lasting recovery needs gold back above US$3,850 to US$3,900, and that won’t happen unless real yields and the dollar ease

“The next tests are the Fed’s meeting on Dec 8 and 9 and US inflation data on Dec 10,” he added.

Alvin Lee, premium client manager at IG Singapore, said the stronger US dollar had added to selling pressure on gold by increasing the opportunity cost of holding the precious metal.

“The general risk off sentiment now is driving investors to hold on to cash and the safe haven status for gold has been called into question recently but for reasons stated above, it seems like the market has a preference for holding cash now,” he said.

The decline in gold prices also weighed on Singapore-listed gold-related stocks.

Shares of gold miner CNMC Goldmine Holdings fell 13.61% over the week to close at 82 cents on Nov 20, down about 60% from their record high of $2.12 in March.

Pawnbroking firms ValueMax Group and MoneyMax Financial Services have also come under pressure in recent months, with their shares falling 25% and nearly 36.6%, respectively, over the past six months.

ValueMax shares fell 8.7% over the week to close at 74 cents on Nov 20, while MoneyMax declined 6.25% to close at 45 cents.

STI dips below 5,000 points, S’pore banks decline

The broader Singapore market also came under pressure on Nov 20, with the benchmark Straits Times Index falling to a six-month low of 4,980.81 before paring some losses to close at 4,972.23 points.

The three local banks were among the decliners, with DBS falling 5.26% over the week to close at $66.11 on Nov 20. OCBC declined 7.3% to $26.54, while UOB lost 6.17% to close at $35.42.

James Ooi, chief market strategist at Tiger Brokers, said hawkish signals from the latest US Federal Reserve meeting minutes and concerns over US restrictions on AI chip exports continued to weigh on investor appetite.

He noted that Singapore’s index heavyweights had benefited from a significant rise in valuations earlier this year, but said the market’s direction would increasingly depend on whether earnings growth could catch up with valuations.

“Companies with access to larger regional and global markets could also offer greater room for expansion and longer-term earnings growth, particularly those with established competitive advantages across multiple markets,” he said.

Home2life lands SGX dual listing

Local furniture company HomesToLife secured its secondary listing on the Singapore Exchange (SGX) Mainboard on Nov 17 with a placement of 7.5 million shares at $1.15 each, raising some $8.6 million in gross proceeds.

The placement attracted more than 50 accredited and institutional investors, including funds under the Equity Market Development Programme.

HomesToLife is the second company to achieve a dual listing on the SGX and Nasdaq, with the first being cybersecurity firm Avepoint in September 2025.

Its furniture is sold by major leading retailers around the world, including DFS in the UK and Cuir Center in France.

Most of the company’s products are made to order, allowing both retail customers and retailers to customise their furniture before they are shipped from factories in China, Vietnam and India.

A number of retailers also carry the brand’s white-label products, which are developed and designed exclusively for the retailers’ territories.

For its 2025 financial year ended Dec 31, Europe accounted for almost 60% of its revenue at $377.9 million, while 26.9% stemmed from Asia-Pacific, and the rest from North America.

HomesToLife reported $19.4 million in operating profit for FY2025, a 103.7% increase from the previous year. But it also faced cost pressures due to disruptions in the Suez Canal, which raised freight rates by 22%.

Shares of HomesToLife closed flat at $1.10 on Nov 20.

What to look out for in the coming week

Singapore’s consumer price index data for October will be released on Nov 23, followed by third-quarter 2026 GDP figures on Nov 24.

data.title: Japan’s core inflation accelerates in October, cementing rate hike expectations
data.description:
TOKYO – Japan’s annual core inflation accelerated in October and exceeded the central bank’s 2% target for the second straight month, a sign of broadening price pressures that cements the case for a near-term interest rate increase.

The data will be among factors the Bank of Japan (BOJ) will scrutinise at its next two-day policy meeting ending on Dec 18, when many market players expect the central bank to raise its policy rate to 1.5% from the current 1.25%.

The core consumer price index (CPI), which strips away the effect of volatile fresh food, rose 2.2% in October from a year earlier, data showed on Nov 20, compared with a median market forecast for a 2.3% gain.

It followed a 2.1% rise in September.

An index that strips away the effects of both volatile fresh food and fuel, which is closely watched by the BOJ as a better gauge of demand-driven price pressures, rose 2.2% in October from a year earlier after increasing 2.4% in September.

Marcel Thieliant, head of Asia-Pacific at Capital Economics, expects inflation, excluding fresh food and energy, to accelerate sharply over the coming months as firms continue to pass on rising raw material costs.

“The upshot is that we now expect the Bank of Japan to lift rates to 2.5% by the middle of next year,” he wrote in a research note.

With stubbornly high energy costs and rising import prices from a weak yen adding to inflationary pressures, the BOJ raised its policy rate to 1.25% in September after delivering a hike in June – a shorter interval than the roughly twice-a-year hikes in 2024 and 2025.

The central bank kept rates steady in October, declaring victory in its 14-year battle to hit its price target. REUTERS

data.title: Anthropic’s US$1.5 trillion debut rewrites venture capital’s playbook
data.description:
For decades, venture capital thrived on small bets that became billion-dollar companies.

Then came Anthropic, rewriting the playbook and forcing investors to write fatter cheques to buy stakes at unheard-of valuations.

The AI lab’s shares began trading on the Nasdaq on Nov 19 at a US$1.5 trillion (S$1.94 trillion) valuation, delivering multibillion-dollar windfalls to venture investors at a moment when the industry needs fresh liquidity to fund more bets on AI companies.

The stock closed at US$97.17, up 17% from its IPO price of $83.

Anthropic’s stock market value ended the day at about US$1.3 trillion, based on its outstanding shares, or US$1.8 trillion, based on its fully diluted shares.

To join the fundraising frenzy, especially at later stages, venture capital firms invested billions, tapping their own investors for additional capital through special-purpose vehicles.

Menlo, Spark reap big returns

Menlo Ventures and Spark Capital emerged with some of the biggest returns by multiple.

Spark Capital was the first venture capital firm to lead an Anthropic investment, in a US$450 million Series C round in 2023 at a valuation of US$4.5 billion.

Spark general partner Yasmin Razavi, who spearheaded the investment, remains the only investor who sits on Anthropic’s board.

Writing the largest cheque in the firm’s history, early-stage firm Menlo invested over US$1 billion for a stake of nearly 1.5%, according to a person familiar with the investment. At a US$1.5 trillion market cap, Menlo’s stake is worth over US$20 billion.

To invest beyond the capacity of its existing fund, Menlo raised a US$750 million special-purpose vehicle from limited partners, a tactic that became increasingly common as funding rounds grew, given the capital needs of AI companies.

Late-stage bets paid off

Sequoia Capital, long known for its early bets, joined a later round and still stands to earn billions of dollars.

Sequoia passed on Anthropic at lower prices. After a leadership change, it wrote its first cheque at the start of 2026, joining a round led by Singapore’s GIC and Coatue at a US$380 billion post-money valuation in February.

It later co-led, alongside Altimeter, Dragoneer and Greenoaks, a round at US$965 billion. Sequoia has invested US$3 billion in Anthropic and continued to invest more through Anthropic’s IPO, signalling further conviction in the AI lab.

Lightspeed Venture Partners, which invested more than US$3 billion in Anthropic, now holds over 2% of the company, making it the largest financial investor in the company, according to two people familiar with the matter.

The returns are possible because of the rapid rise in Anthropic’s valuation and revenue.

Its annualised revenue grew from about US$1 billion at the start of 2025 to about US$81 billion in October, as its valuation climbed from US$61.5 billion in March 2025 to US$965 billion in the latest private round this May.

Strategic backers, too, supply much of the unprecedented capital and computing power needed by AI labs.

The combined stake of Amazon and Alphabet’s Google in Anthropic is about 28.4%.

“We’re living through a very unique time of profound change happening at a higher velocity than ever before,” said Will Griffith, a partner at Iconiq, which has invested US$6.1 billion, making the fund the second-largest financial investor by ownership in Anthropic.

“The scale of the impact of these businesses and the breadth of market opportunities is larger than anything we’ve seen before.

“And that is going to afford investment opportunities that are larger than what we’ve seen in the past.” REUTERS

data.title: South Korea’s exports top US$1 trillion for first time on chip boom
data.description:
SEOUL – South Korea’s annual exports surpassed US$1 trillion (S$1.29 trillion) for the first time, making it the fourth country to reach the milestone after Germany, the US and China, and the first new entrant to the club in 19 years, as global spending on artificial intelligence sent semiconductor prices and shipments soaring.

Cumulative exports crossed the mark at 2.09pm on Nov 19, a year after first topping US$700 billion and 62 years after reaching US$100 million.

President Lee Jae Myung hailed the achievement as the culmination of generations of effort, paying tribute to workers who spent their youth in garment factories, shoe manufacturers and shipyards.

“The gains from exports must, above all, improve people’s lives,” he said in a message on X, pledging to ensure that growth benefits large and small companies and communities across the country.

“We must now turn this achievement into sustained growth. We will strengthen the competitiveness of our key industries and nurture future growth engines such as AI and biotechnology,” he said.

“We will also actively support Korean consumer products, including beauty products and food, as they expand into global markets.”

Germany and the US crossed the US$1 trillion mark in 2006, followed by China in 2007, riding a trade boom after China joined the World Trade Organization.

South Korea did so amid rising tariffs and the US-China rivalry, with a population of 51.6 million and an economy of just US$1.88 trillion, smaller than any of its predecessors at the time.

The Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources projects full-year exports of US$1.17 trillion, up about 65% from a record US$709.3 billion in 2025.

“Given our smaller population and economy, this is a remarkable achievement,” Kang Kam-chan, the ministry’s deputy minister for trade and investment, told reporters.

Chips lead, but not alone

Exports totalled US$930.2 billion in the first 10 months, including US$396.8 billion in semiconductors, accounting for about 43% of the total and nearly triple the previous record for the period.

AI data centre demand drove up DRAM and NAND prices, while the build-out lifted shipments of solid-state drives, transformers, cables and copper, according to the ministry.

Exports excluding chips rose 20%, with 16 of 20 major categories gaining. Cosmetics exports reached US$12.4 billion, topping the 2025 full-year record in 10 months.

Shipments rose in seven of nine major markets, led by China, up 88%, and the US, up 77%.

Small and mid-sized companies also posted record exports.

Imports rose 21% to US$635.1 billion, leaving a surplus of about US$295 billion through October, against US$77.4 billion for all of 2025.

“Part of the US$1 trillion belongs to imports,” Kang said, citing steady supplies of crude oil, naphtha and chipmaking equipment.

Bigger numbers, thinner spread

Much of the record reflects higher prices, not higher output.

Kang said rising prices drove much of the growth, as AI demand sent memory chip prices soaring and petroleum product export prices jumped 62% to US$1,105 a tonne.

He acknowledged the gains have gone mostly to large companies, citing structural limits in chips and petrochemicals, which have short supply chains and employ relatively few workers, unlike automobiles or ships.

“It is regrettable that the profits have not flowed through to suppliers,” he said, adding that new chip plants and joint research with equipment makers could spread the benefits.

Normally, a large trade surplus lifts the won as exporters convert their dollar earnings into local currency. But many keep those dollars abroad or spend them on imported parts and overseas factories, meaning less of the surplus reaches the currency market.

From selling goods to investing abroad

Kang said exports could exceed US$1 trillion again in 2027, though easing chip and oil prices could pull them below the 2026 level.

He expects AI infrastructure demand to hold through the third quarter of 2027.

Delays in US data centre projects, Chinese competition and protectionism remain risks.

He said South Korea’s major industries appear to be undergoing a structural shift.

When exports first passed US$10 billion in 1977, they were led by ships, frozen fish, plywood and clothing.

The AI build-out now creates markets for South Korean power equipment, copper and aluminium alongside chips.

That shift, he said, calls for rethinking how South Korea manages its surpluses. Japan, Germany and China channelled theirs into overseas investments that now return income home.

“As an economy matures and costs rise, it cannot keep expanding production at home indefinitely,” Kang said. “The export structure has to gradually shift towards investment.”

He sees overseas investment as a way to build strategic ties, particularly with partners sensitive to trade deficits, such as the US, where the administration of Donald Trump has made shrinking them a priority.

South Korean factories abroad can create local jobs, buy from local suppliers and export to third markets, giving partners a stake in the relationship.

“Korea should not be a country that simply sells goods,” he said.

Asked whether South Korea would follow Japan, which came to rely on income from overseas investment after the 1985 Plaza Accord, Kang said his country is likely to take a similar path.

But he noted that Japanese companies prospered while ordinary Japanese saw fewer gains.

South Korea should instead keep research and “mother factories”, the advanced plants that develop new processes, at home while expanding overseas, he said.
THE KOREA HERALD/ASIA NEWS NETWORK

data.title: AI-fuelled cyberattacks drive claims surge at Japan insurers
data.description:
Japan’s biggest property insurers are reporting a sharp jump in cyberinsurance claims as artificial intelligence-driven attacks grow more sophisticated and hacking incidents surge nationwide.

Tokio Marine Holdings received three times as many cyberinsurance claim notifications in October as usual, according to the company. Sompo Holdings said claims in October were running at 2½ times higher than the average over the one-year period ending Sept 30, 2026. Both insurers disclosed the figures at earnings briefings on Nov 19. 

Attackers are using increasingly sophisticated methods as AI advances, and unauthorised access has led to a string of personal data leaks in Japan. The increase in claims raises the risk of costly payouts even as rising numbers of incidents fuel demand for protection. 

Payouts on cyberpolicies could rise, but the surge has yet to translate into a significant earnings hit. Yoshinari Endo, a managing executive officer at Tokio Marine, said his company expects some impact on full-year results, though it is managing the profit risk and expects losses to stay within the assumptions of its initial annual plan. 

Junsuke Koike, an executive vice-president at Sompo, said inquiries about raising coverage amounts or adding coverage items had tripled from normal levels.

Japan’s experience mirrors a broader rise in cyberclaims globally. US insurers reported more than 56,000 cyberclaims in 2025, up 20% from a year earlier, while large companies are facing increasingly costly incidents. Cyberpolicies typically cover damages owed for data breaches, recovery costs and profits lost from disruptions, making insurance a growing part of corporate risk management. 

Cyberinsurance penetration in Japan remains low for smaller companies. A 2025 survey by the General Insurance Association of Japan found that only 8.8% of small- and medium-sized business owners said they had cyberinsurance as a defence against attacks.

Yasuko Fukuda, a senior executive officer at MS&AD Insurance Group Holdings, said at an earnings briefing on Nov 19 that there is “significant room for the market to expand”.

The insurers are trying to limit losses by helping customers prevent attacks. Starting in December, Sompo will offer a new service with Trend Micro and others that monitors for vulnerabilities on the internet.

Insurers are being selective about underwriting. Tokio Marine may cap payouts or tighten coverage terms depending on a customer’s risk profile, Endo said. The company expects its cyberinsurance business to remain profitable in the fiscal year through March 2027. Standard total payout limits in Japan and overseas run from about 100 million yen (S$812,000) to several hundred million yen per contract. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Indonesia revokes Riau forestry permits of APRIL Group unit over alleged peatland fires, violations
data.description:
JAKARTA – Indonesia has revoked forestry permits covering 338,536ha held by Riau Andalan Pulp and Paper (RAPP), a subsidiary of Asia Pacific Resources International Limited (APRIL) Group.

The move, which affects an area about 4.5 times the size of Singapore, was taken over alleged environmental violations, including recurring peatland fires, illegal plantations and damage to protected areas, the government’s forest enforcement task force said on Nov 20.

The enforcement push comes amid heightened scrutiny of companies linked to forest fires and transboundary haze; the latest move marks a significant crackdown on major corporate players in the forestry sector.

The permits were revoked under a Forestry Ministerial Decree dated Nov 19, with the entire concession area in Riau province returning to state control, said the Forest Area Enforcement Task Force, known as Satgas PKH, in a statement on Nov 20.

“All activities within the revoked concession areas have been halted, while the government has taken back control of the land,” it added. “The revocation does not absolve the company of its environmental restoration obligations or potential legal liabilities.”

The task force cited recurring peatland fires, oil palm plantations spanning 18,362.74ha, unauthorised mining activities covering 541.46ha, and damage to protected areas spanning 211.54ha as grounds for the revocation.

It also raised concerns over the protection of areas surrounding Tesso Nilo National Park, which provides habitat for endangered Sumatran elephants.

APRIL Group said it learnt about the government’s decision through media reports. It added that it was awaiting formal notification and further clarification from authorities.

“We respect the authority of the government and will continue to communicate constructively with the relevant authorities,” the company said in a statement. It added that it would respond through the appropriate channels once it received formal notification. THE BUSINESS TIMES

data.title: Anthropic’s listing draws massive interest from S’pore retail investors, but valuation fears remain
data.description:
SINGAPORE – Forget the doom and gloom of an impending AI bubble bursting and the uncertainty of a post-Jensen Huang world. When it came to Anthropic’s record-breaking debut on Wall Street, Singapore investors were ravenous and had no intention of missing out.

Online brokerages told The Straits Times that interest had swelled well ahead of the Nov 19 listing, and Anthropic was the most-traded stock on its debut day, with trading activity exceeding Elon Musk’s SpaceX in June.

Anthropic’s initial public offering (IPO), the second blockbuster of 2026, was six to seven times oversubscribed and raised US$81.3 billion (S$104.8 billion), beating SpaceX’s raising of US$75 billion in June.

Anthropic opened on Nasdaq at US$111.50 – 34.3% higher than its IPO price of US$83. Its market value briefly exceeded US$2 trillion in intraday trading before closing the day at US$97.17, with a market capitalisation of US$1.8 trillion.

Some observers may say it was perhaps not the best time for the developer of the AI model Claude to launch its IPO.

Sentiment about AI weakened as investors grew increasingly cautious about massive capital expenditures, which has sent tech stocks tumbling since October.

Its Wall Street debut also came days after Jensen Huang, CEO of chipmaking giant Nvidia, resigned, casting a pall of uncertainty over the future of AI and the semiconductor industry.

Anthropic itself had also laid out over 90 pages of risk factors to its operations in its prospectus, the most frightening of which was the catastrophic risks its AI tech posed to humanity.

But all the fears and controversy did not deter retail investors hungry for a slice of the AI pie, and Anthropic passed a seemingly challenging test of investor appetite with flying colours.

Anthropic’s stock churned out more retail trading activity on its public debut than any other stock on its listing day going back to 2012, according to data from US-based financial research firm Vanda Research.

Investors traded US$772 million worth of Anthropic shares, exceeding the US$669 million recorded during SpaceX’s first trading session in June.

In Singapore, investor appetite was just as voracious.

“Anthropic was the clear focus of US trading on Syfe,” said the platform’s managing director and group head of investment and advisory Ritesh Ganeriwal.

Pre-orders on the platform were double those for SpaceX, and nearly half of Syfe customers who traded US stocks that day traded Anthropic’s.

Anthropic made up about one in four US stock trades on Syfe, making it the platform’s most-traded US stock. It drew more than twice as many trades as Nvidia, the second most-traded stock.

Syfe added that 83% of Anthropic trades were market orders, compared with about 65% for US trades normally.

According to Moomoo, Anthropic single-handedly captured around 48% of total trade count and 45% of total trading value across the platform’s trading basket of the AI company and Magnificent Seven stocks that comprise the largest US tech companies.

Retail investors were more inclined to buy than sell the stock, suggesting they were accumulating shares rather than flipping them the same day, a Moomoo analyst said. Buy activity on the company’s stock outpaced sell activity by nearly four to one in trade count.

On Longbridge Securities’ platform, Anthropic shares recorded a trading value around 4.5 times the average for the Magnificent Seven stocks.

A better or more uncertain outlook?

Analysts say Anthropic’s debut was largely a success, but questions remain over whether it can sustain its first-day momentum.

Even though it closed 17% above its IPO price, it was still significantly below its opening price of US$111.50, demonstrating the volatility that investors can face during a strong debut.

“Investors wanted Anthropic, but they would not pay any price for it,” said Syfe’s Ganeriwal.

“Price trajectory will be closely watched as a signal of institutional conviction in AI at current valuations. The broader AI sector’s decline yesterday may reflect scepticism around the durability of the AI trade, though a single data point does not constitute a trend,” said the Moomoo analyst.

Anthropic reported steep losses of over US$80 billion for the first half of 2026, but it was still able to attract significant investor capital, indicating that a great deal of the company’s future success has already been priced in, said UOB Kay Hian’s director of wealth management Kenneth Goh.

Investors will now be monitoring the company’s performance to assess if its valuation had been overinflated, and this will hinge on its ability to carve out a strong enterprise business.

Lorraine Tan, Morningstar director of equity research for Asia, said it is not unusual for industries in the build-out phase to still attract investors while running a loss. Amazon notably made net losses from its listing in 1997 until 2003.

Despite giving a “Very High” uncertainty rating on Anthropic, Tan noted the company’s revenue has a compound annual growth rate of 46.5% and forecasts its capital expenditure to peak in 2028, with free cash flow turning positive in 2030.

“We believe Anthropic will be able to grow Claude’s use case to more industries, and we also see Claude as being able to carve out its position in AI tools for enterprises,” said Tan, adding that Anthropic is unlikely to play in the mass market space for AI tools which will likely see much more competition.

In the meantime, Ganeriwal said investors trading Anthropic’s stock should consider three key factors: volatility of newly listed stocks while the markets settle on a value; growth against cost; and the pace at which the company’s competitors are improving their capabilities, which can quickly shift pricing.

Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund GIC’s sizeable stake in Anthropic should also offer retail investors another vote of confidence. It has invested more than US$4.5 billion over three funding rounds, including a US$65 billion Series H round, which it co-led in May.

GIC’s stake is now worth around US$15 billion at Anthropic’s IPO price.

Chris Emanuel, managing director and head of GIC’s technology investment group, said in a LinkedIn post on Nov 20 that the fund was now one of Anthropic’s largest investors.

“An IPO is an important milestone, but it’s just one moment in a company’s journey,” he said. “We invest across multiple rounds, through the IPO and beyond. That’s life-cycle investing in practice.”

UOB Kay Hian’s Goh said GIC’s investment in three rounds over nine months illustrates “a quick pace for an institution of its size”, and Singapore investors could see indirect benefits.

“A gain like this strengthens the reserves, and returns on the reserves help fund the Budget. The local stock market offers little direct exposure to AI, so holdings like this are one way Singapore takes part.”

Gavin Chia, Singapore and regional chief executive officer at Longbridge Securities, cautioned retail investors against interpreting GIC’s participation as an “automatic endorsement of the stock at its current valuation”.

This is because institutional investors operate with different investment mandates, risk tolerances and portfolio structures. GIC’s entry terms, portfolio size, diversification and mandate would therefore differ significantly from those of an individual.

“The lesson retail investors can draw from GIC is not necessarily which company to invest in, but how to approach long-term opportunities: with conviction, discipline and a clear understanding of the risks involved. In a rapidly evolving industry like AI, that long-term perspective becomes particularly valuable.”

Next-day market falls

Despite Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO and Nvidia’s strong earnings on Nov 17, Asian markets slumped on Nov 20 as technology stocks opened lower to extend a global rout.

The sell-off hit chipmakers and semiconductor suppliers that have been some of the largest beneficiaries of the AI boom.

South Korea’s Kospi closed 5% lower on the back of losses by Samsung and SK Hynix, while Japan’s Nikkei 225 also fell 5%. Both the Straits Times Index and Hong Kong’s Hang Seng slid around 2%.

The declines followed losses on Wall Street, with both Nasdaq and the S&P 500 dropping more than 2%.

“This looks more like a valuation and financing reset than an immediate collapse in AI earnings,” Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo Singapore, wrote in a note.

Ganeriwal noted that interest rates and not AI demand were the main driver for the current weaker mood across markets, with expectations of a rate hike by the US Federal Reserve in December now rising.

“The AI build-out needs enormous financing, and money is getting more expensive. That hurts companies that borrow to build far more than those funding it from their own cash flow.”

data.title: Singapore-based DayOne to pause US IPO plans on data centre, market concerns: Sources
data.description:
SINGAPORE – DayOne Data Centers has put plans for its multibillion-dollar US initial public offering (IPO) on hold, sources familiar with the matter said, as investors question the sustainability of frothy valuations for digital infrastructure supporting the artificial intelligence boom.

The data centre operator, whose biggest customer is ByteDance, the Chinese owner of TikTok, was initially intending to raise as much as US$5 billion (S$6.5 billion) from an IPO as soon as the fourth quarter, Bloomberg News reported previously.

But the company started to reassess options including a delay or a smaller listing as volatility increased around data centres and AI stocks.

Singapore-based DayOne may still pursue an IPO in 2027 if the situation and market sentiment improves, the sources said, asking not to be identified because the information is not public.

The company filed for the IPO in October and has been working with Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Citigroup and BNP Paribas on the listing.

Deliberations are ongoing and no final decisions on the IPO have been made, the sources said.

A representative for DayOne declined to comment.

Doubts about the potential payoff from massive investments into AI have fuelled volatility in global markets.

The Nasdaq 100 has dropped more than 6% in November, heading for its worst November performance since 2008.

Still, Anthropic staged a record-breaking US$107.3 billion IPO and private placement, and rose 17% on its trading debut on Nov 19, becoming the world’s seventh-most valuable company.

Other data centre-related companies have either pulled or delayed their IPO plans amid investor concerns in the sector.

In October, Firmus Grid abandoned its attempt at one of Australia’s biggest-ever IPOs, while Blackstone-backed AirTrunk is delaying a listing of a real estate investment trust in Singapore until 2027.

DayOne has hyperscale facilities in countries including Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia, which have seen a boom in data centre development fuelled by demand from Chinese tech companies like ByteDance and Alibaba Group.

The US in November put interim rules on those four countries to restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips and servers, telling data centre operators that they will need a licence to purchase American tech hardware.

DayOne’s backers include Coatue, Hillhouse, GDS Holdings, SoftBank Vision Fund and Citadel’s Ken Griffin. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Stocks slide as AI sell-off deepens; Asia has worst week since 2020
data.description:
LONDON/HONG KONG/SINGAPORE – Stock markets stumbled around the world on Nov 20 after Anthropic’s initial public offering failed to restore investors’ faith in the AI sector, with US futures dropping and Asian shares heading for their worst week since 2020.

Government bonds rallied as investors sought safe-haven assets.

Shares of Anthropic, the world’s first publicly traded frontier artificial intelligence company, jumped as it launched the biggest IPO in history on Nov 19, although they pared gains later in the session and were down 10% in pre-market trading on Nov 20.

The debut did little to revive excitement over the broader AI theme, however, as investors continued to question whether the huge amounts of spending would deliver returns.

“The Anthropic IPO gave us some brief respite from the cloud of negativity,” said Michael Field, chief equity strategist at Morningstar. “That pause is well and truly over unfortunately.”

Futures for the tech-focused Nasdaq 100 fell 2% after the index dropped the same amount on Nov 19. The Nasdaq is now down around 15% since hitting a record high in early October.

S&P 500 futures were in the red after the index fell for a sixth straight session on Nov 19. A seven-day run of declines would be the worst streak since the pandemic.

The STOXX 600 gauge of European stocks fell almost 2%, while MSCI’s world index of stocks fell for a seventh straight session, its longest losing streak since 2023.

The MSCI index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan tumbled and has sunk 8% this week, its worst performance since the Covid-19 pandemic in March 2020.

Nvidia’s blowout earnings earlier in the week and Anthropic’s IPO have both failed to restore confidence, said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at bank and investment firm Saxo.

“The market is no longer looking for proof of AI demand alone,” she said. “It wants evidence that the extraordinary spending across the ecosystem can generate sustainable returns.”

The VIX index of expected volatility on Wall Street stocks jumped and traded at its highest since March on Nov 20.

Adding to the unease, a report on AMD from a media outlet associated with short-selling fund Hunterbrook Capital raised concerns that the chipmaker’s ties to Chinese entities, some linked to blacklisted firms, could draw greater US regulatory scrutiny to the sector.

“No one headline drove the roll, though some pointed to an AMD short report which tapered overall sentiment,” said Goldman Sachs analysts in a trading note.

All of that has piled further pressure on the AI trade, already battered in recent weeks by Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia and growing anti-data-centre sentiment exemplified by the Democrats’ sweep of the US midterm elections.

Japan’s Nikkei tumbled 5%. Taiwanese shares were down 17% for the week, their biggest weekly decline since 1990.

Despite the sharp drop in stocks, however, equity markets remain up for the year after a blistering rally in the first half on AI optimism.

Treasuries rally as investors take cover

US Treasuries rallied as stocks took a beating, sending investors towards assets deemed safe havens.

The yield on benchmark 10-year Treasury notes fell for a fifth straight session, to below 5%, while German 10-year bond yields fell 10 basis points (bps), the most since April. Bond yields move inversely to prices.

Meanwhile, the US dollar held steady at around its highest level in 20 months, also garnering support from growing expectations of a more hawkish Federal Reserve.

Fed funds futures imply that a quarter-point rate hike in December is essentially locked in.

Oil prices were steady, with Brent crude futures trading at US$90 a barrel and on track for a third week of declines. REUTERS

data.title: Anthropic pulled off the biggest IPO ever. What that means, by the numbers
data.description:
Anthropic has made a superlative-filled debut on Wall Street, breaking all records for money raised on Wall Street as it became the first major artificial intelligence lab to become a publicly traded company.

The price tag on its shares was enough to put the value of the San Francisco company well beyond US$1 trillion (S$1.29 trillion).

That kind of number was once unheard of for a company’s first moments trading on the stock market. But an acceleration in corporate wealth – and most recently the AI boom – has changed that.

Anthropic is the second business to debut with a value over a trillion dollars, following SpaceX just months ago, and will join a handful of other tech giants that measure their wealth by figures reaching 13 digits.

Time will tell how Anthropic ultimately fares on the public market. The Claude maker decided to proceed with its IPO despite jitters among some investors over market volatility, fears of a possible AI bubble and growing unease among the public about the technology’s risks overall.

Here are some numbers to help understand the IPO on Nov 19.

The amount in proceeds raised by the offering: US$81 billion

That makes Anthropic’s debut the biggest ever. Ahead of trading on Nov 19, it offered 980 million shares priced at US$83 each, putting Anthropic ahead of Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which set a previous record with its IPO proceeds of about US$75 billion in June.

The next biggest IPO hauls went to South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix US$26.5 billion in July and oil giant Saudi Aramco US$25.6 billion in 2019.

Anthropic’s initial valuation: US$1.5 trillion

The initial price per share was set at US$83. But that spiked more than 30% to open at US$111.50 a share – pushing the company’s total valuation by half a trillion dollars to US$2.01 trillion just before noon Eastern time (1am Singapore time on Nov 20).

By market close on Nov 19, Anthropic finished its first trading day at US$97.17 per share. That is still over 17% higher than its initial public offering price, and amounts to a market value of roughly US$1.75 trillion.

In June, SpaceX ended its first day of trading on the public market with a valuation of US$2.1 trillion. Its market cap has since fallen to closer to US$1.95 trillion.

Number of public companies that have reached the trillion-dollar club in the S&P 500: 11

Apple currently leads the pack at US$5.1 trillion, followed by Microsoft (US$3.8 trillion) and Nvidia (US$3.6 trillion), among others. That does not count SpaceX and Anthropic, which also have joined the trillion-dollar club even though they are not in the S&P 500 index yet.

Only in recent memory have major corporations been valued over US$1 trillion. iPhone maker Apple was the first to pass that threshold, back in 2018.

How far a trillion US dollar bills would stretch if laid end to end: 156 million kilometres

That would surpass the roughly 150 million kilometres between Earth and the sun.

The number “one trillion” is hard in itself for the human mind to comprehend. US$1 trillion is a thousand times greater than US$1 billion. And a million times more than US$1 million.

There are more than 8.2 billion people living on Earth today, per the US Census Bureau. If US$1 trillion was divided among the entire population, each person would receive almost US$122. AP

data.title: Wall Street ends sharply lower as Anthropic’s debut fails to revive AI fervour
data.description:
NEW YORK - US stocks slumped on Nov 19, after Anthropic’s super-sized IPO failed to revitalise faded enthusiasm over artificial intelligence, as an early spike in its share price ebbed.

All three major US stock indexes ended the session sharply lower, with the benchmark S&P 500 logging its fifth straight session of losses.

The S&P 500 was on course to post its steepest weekly loss since April 2025.

Anthropic’s debut, the largest IPO on record, was priced late on Nov 18 at US$83 per share and was widely viewed as the next high bar to clear for the AI trade.

The stock opened at US$111.50 shortly before noon.

After the company’s market valuation briefly surpassed US$2 trillion (S$2.5 trillion), its momentum began to lose steam.

“The Anthropic IPO is attracting gobs of attention,” said Jed Ellerbroek, portfolio manager at Argent Capital in St Louis, Missouri.

“That money is coming from somewhere; investors are making changes in their portfolio to incorporate Anthropic, so I wouldn’t extrapolate a whole lot of meaning from today’s trading behaviour, whether it’s up or down.”

Even so, Ellerbroek’s enthusiasm for the AI trade has waned.

“My beliefs about the growth in data centre capex spending have come down a little bit over the last month or two,” he added.

“Nvidia’s crisis situation is a big deal. The midterm elections have had an impact.”

“Data centres are going to be more expensive to build, and they’re going to be built more slowly.”

Advanced Micro Devices shares tumbled after investigative outlet Hunterbrook said its affiliated fund, Hunterbrook Capital, had taken a short position in the company.

Most chipmakers were lower, including Micron and Broadcom, among others.

Nvidia marked its sixth straight session of losses after the chipmaker’s upbeat revenue forecast did little to lift sentiment.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index closed lower.

Neocloud firms CoreWeave and Nebius sustained steep losses.

In other stocks, Palo Alto Networks shares jumped after the cybersecurity firm raised its 2027 revenue guidance.

Walmart dipped after the retail giant’s annual sales forecast disappointed investors.

According to preliminary data, the S&P 500 lost 148.39 points, or 2.03%, to end at 7,175.24 points, while the Nasdaq Composite lost 544.00 points, or 2.23%, to 23,885.88.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1,102.71 points, or 2.20%, to 49,095.46.

Focus turns to the US Fed

Following the Nov 18 release of minutes from the US Federal Reserve’s October policy meeting, investors are recalibrating their expectations pertaining to upcoming rate decisions.

The minutes revealed a desire to rein in inflation even prior to the recent release of consumer and producer price indexes, which showed price pressures heating up.

Financial markets are currently pricing in about a 94% likelihood of a 25-basis-point rate hike at the central bank’s December meeting, with a small but growing chance of a super-sized 50-basis-point increase, according to CME’s FedWatch tool.

Next week, the Commerce Department is expected to release its personal consumption expenditures (PCE) report, which includes the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, the PCE price index. Analysts expect the report to show year-on-year core inflation of 3.2%, well above the central bank’s 2% annual target. REUTERS

data.title: JPMorgan, Visa, Mastercard say third-party vendors targeted in cyberattack
data.description:
NEW YORK - JPMorgan Chase, the largest US lender, said on Nov 19 that third parties who provide services to the firm were the target of a cyberattack.

“Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses,” a JPMorgan spokesperson said, adding that the company would be contacting the affected customers directly.

“There is no connection to service disruption of some customers experienced earlier this week,” the spokesperson added.

Earlier this week, the bank experienced problems processing transactions due to a software bug which also affected other banks and caused some disruptions.

These incidents at JPMorgan followed several other recent problems including a nationwide FAA ground stop that disrupted travel last week and Microsoft’s global email outage, while in October crypto exchange Binance experienced a massive hack.

After the outage, lenders received inquiries from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), according to an industry executive, who added that the US banking regulator was trying to assess the impact and wanted to know about communication to customers.

The Treasury and the OCC were calling banks minutes after the incident was reported to check that the issue was contained and it was not a cyber-related incident, a second person said, adding that the OCC routinely checks after any such incidents.

“Customers don’t distinguish between a bank and a vendor when it comes to a cyberattack, so there is a question of reputational risk here,” said Carissa Robb, of SolomonEdwards, a consulting firm.

“There needs to be a little bit more pressure on how often companies are scrutinising the amount of data that is shared with vendors and the necessity of the data being shared,” Robb said.

A cyber extortion group called “n0n” claimed on Nov 16 to have obtained cardmember engagement records that included “hundreds of thousands of campaign interactions for tens of thousands of distinct cardmember email addresses,” according to a screenshot of the message captured by cybercrime research platform eCrime.ch.

The data includes what appears to be 124 bank employee email addresses and more than 16,000 customer email addresses, some with phone numbers and postal codes, according to a Reuters review.

Reuters could not independently verify the authenticity of the data.

JPMorgan declined to comment on the data.

The same hacking group on Nov 16 posted similar claims regarding Visa and Mastercard and posted data.

A Visa spokesperson said the company is aware of the claims and that they are “associated with an incident involving a third-party service provider in Asia Pacific. Visa’s systems were not involved and were not impacted. No payments data such as card numbers were affected.”

A Mastercard spokesperson said the company was recently informed of an incident “at a third-party provider that resulted in the exposure of limited amount of email addresses – non-payments information – from a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit programme. There is no impact to the Mastercard payment network or the ability for people to use their cards.”

The Visa data posted by the group appears to be primarily focused on Asian-Pacific markets, including Hong Kong, Taiwan, Korea, Japan, Philippines, Singapore, Malaysia, Australia, Macau and others, according to a Reuters review.

Across several spreadsheets, the data includes thousands of purported customer email addresses, phone numbers, and Visa marketing campaign data.

Reuters has not verified the authenticity of the data.

The Mastercard data posted by n0n includes marketing data related to customers in North America, the Middle East and Africa, and a small number of Mastercard employee email addresses.

The hacking group has claimed roughly 200 incidents since emerging in September 2026, according to eCrime.ch. REUTERS

data.title: Anthropic soars 34% to US$2 trillion valuation on Wall Street debut
data.description:
NEW YORK - Anthropic shares soared more than 34% in their Nasdaq debut on Nov 19, pushing the AI giant’s value to about US$2 trillion (S$2.5 trillion) as investors shrugged off the Nvidia spy scandal and fears of a tech bubble.

The shares opened at US$111.50, up from the US$83 at which the company priced its shares on Nov 18, already above its expected range.

Anthropic raised a record US$81.3 billion, selling 980 million shares, about 956 million of them new shares and the rest from existing shareholders. The company itself will receive about US$79.4 billion.

The IPO’s original price valued the maker of the Claude chatbot at about US$1.5 trillion, including employee stock options and restricted shares.

The roughly US$2 trillion valuation at the open matches estimates floated earlier this year, before AI stocks slid on Wall Street.

The debut marks a milestone in the AI boom. A company founded five years ago by OpenAI defectors worried about AI safety has become the first of the leading model developers to list on Wall Street, at a valuation rivalling decades-old tech brands.

The listing, under the ticker “ANT,” gives ordinary investors their first chance to bet directly on a stand-alone AI giant.

“Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so, only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing,” chief executive Dario Amodei said at the Nasdaq in New York’s Times Square, underlining the company’s priority of promoting safe AI.

‘Fresh air’

As is usual for large listings, the shares began trading well after the opening bell, once Nasdaq and the lead investment banks had gathered buy and sell orders to set an opening price.

The offering surpasses the US$75 billion that Elon Musk’s SpaceX raised in its June IPO at a valuation of US$1.77 trillion.

SpaceX’s total ultimately rose to US$86 billion after its underwriters exercised an option to buy additional shares. SpaceX shares opened 11% above their IPO price.

Anthropic has granted its underwriters an option to buy up to 147 million more shares, which would lift its total to about US$93.5 billion.

“Demand seems to be outstripping supply of this newly publicly traded company,” Art Hogan of B. Riley Wealth Management told AFP.

“This may be the breath of fresh air that the tech trade needed to move beyond the fog of artificial intelligence that we’ve been living in for the last couple of weeks,” he added.

The strong demand comes even as AI stocks have swung sharply, with investors questioning whether heavy spending on the technology will pay off.

Nvidia, the chip giant at the centre of the AI investment boom and an investor in Anthropic and dozens of other AI companies, has been shaken by the resignation of chief executive Jensen Huang after a reported affair with a woman suspected by US intelligence to be a Chinese spy.

Anthropic’s Claude models are among the most powerful in the world, hailed for their problem-solving potential but also feared for their capacity to destabilise societies and replace human workers.

The five-year-old company’s revenue has surged at a pace few US companies have ever matched, reaching US$17 billion in the third quarter, up from US$1.4 billion a year earlier.

Much of that revenue comes from customers paying to use its AI models for computer coding.

Amodei and his sister Daniela, the company’s president, founded Anthropic with several colleagues in 2021 after leaving ChatGPT-maker OpenAI.

Threats to Americans

Anthropic’s IPO filing goes into extensive detail on the risks of the technology, reflecting the company’s focus on safety even as it builds ever more powerful models.

It warns that advanced AI systems “could pose catastrophic or existential risks to society if not developed and deployed responsibly.”

US Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren criticised the listing on X, saying the company “fails to answer for the potential threats to Americans’ retirements and the entire financial system if this IPO goes awry.”

About a dozen protesters gathered outside the Nasdaq on Nov 19, chanting: “Why you doing IPO? This AI bubble’s about to blow!” AFP

data.title: US chip equipment maker KLA opens expanded site in Singapore, with plans for further growth
data.description:
SINGAPORE – US semiconductor equipment maker KLA opened an expanded plant in Singapore and announced it has plans for a third phase of expansion, making the Republic one of its major production hubs globally.

The expanded site, Building 22B in Ang Mo Kio, was announced in October 2024 and is now fully operational – giving the company about 210,000 sq ft of new operational space.

KLA, which makes machines and tools such as surface profilers, testers and semiconductor assembly solutions for chipmakers, established its presence in Singapore in 1996 and began manufacturing here in 2006.

Theo Kneepkens, KLA Singapore country president and senior vice-president of global operations, said the company has also outlined plans for a further expansion phase here, subject to finalisation of land arrangements and relevant approvals.

“I was actually hoping that this would already be a ground-breaking of our next phase. But we’re still defining a few details of our next phase of expansion before we can officially announce that,” he said.

“But it’s clear that our next phase of growth will be bigger than the current expanded site.”

Kneepkens said KLA’s plans for an additional phase reflect its conviction that Singapore – with its exceptional talent, supportive governance and strategic position – will remain indispensable in how the world manufactures critical semiconductor equipment powering AI and advanced computing.

In the longer term, Building 22B and the planned phase are expected to support about 1,000 new jobs across research and development, supply chain and manufacturing engineering.

KLA chief financial officer Bren Higgins said: “We’ve added hundreds of new roles, with over 2,200 employees working across multiple shifts, and 90% of KLA Singapore employees are locals, including both Singaporean citizens and permanent residents.”

He noted that KLA’s long-term investment in Singapore has been driven by the local talent, highly collaborative partners and access to suppliers and customers.

“We are experiencing unprecedented growth across the industry, and our customers show no signs of slowing. If anything, the demand environment is only accelerating,” he said.

KLA’s expansion comes on the heels of several investment commitments announced in the past few years by companies that fabricate semiconductors or are part of the manufacturing value chain, such as processors of silicon substrate materials and companies that test, assemble and package chips.

Chip firms that have made fresh investments include GlobalFoundries, Micron, Siltronic, Soitec, UMC, Vanguard International Semiconductor and NXP Semiconductors.

Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said at KLA’s opening ceremony that Singapore has built a strong ecosystem for semiconductor equipment manufacturing, and the Republic now accounts for around one-fifth of global production.

“Singapore must keep building the specialised capabilities that companies need to compete.

“By working with partners like KLA, we can support their growth while creating good opportunities for our people and enterprises,” he said.

Gan, who is also Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry (Trade), said that as chips become more powerful and specialised, manufacturing them requires greater precision.

Hence, equipment made by companies like KLA, which can measure process variations and detect defects early, is increasingly important.

“KLA is a key part of Singapore’s strength in this field. Its process-control tools help chipmakers bring advanced technologies into reliable, high-volume production,” he added.

He said Singapore is also investing in the research capabilities needed to seize new opportunities in the chip industry, committing $800 million under the Research, Innovation and Enterprise 2030 plan to the RIE Flagship in Semiconductors.

He lauded a three-year collaboration between KLA and A*STAR’s Institute of Microelectronics, saying such partnerships will help turn research into practical manufacturing solutions, so Singapore can continue to meet the semiconductor industry’s changing needs.

Local suppliers are evolving alongside the multinational companies they support, Gan added.

He cited precision engineering firm Sys-Mac Automation Engineering, which has strengthened its capabilities and shortened prototype development timelines in partnership with KLA.

Sys-Mac is also investing in new cleanroom capabilities to support KLA’s next-generation systems.

Gan added: “As our people and enterprises deepen their expertise, they can take on more demanding work and help companies like KLA grow from Singapore. And as KLA grows, it will in turn create more opportunities for our enterprises and people.”

Cindy Koh, executive vice-president at the Singapore Economic Development Board, said: “The opening of KLA’s latest manufacturing facility will deepen Singapore’s capabilities in semiconductor equipment development and create quality jobs for Singaporeans in manufacturing engineering and R&D, alongside training and upskilling opportunities.”

data.title: Alibaba tops revenue estimates on AI cloud growth; profit up on investment gains
data.description:
Alibaba beat estimates for September-quarter revenue on Nov 19 as demand for its AI cloud services surged, while investment gains helped more than triple reported profit.

China’s biggest e-commerce company by market share said revenue from AI cloud and computing services jumped 53%, highlighting the growing payoff from heavy investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure and products.

“This quarter, our business delivered strong growth in both revenue and earnings because of our strategic focus on AI + Cloud growth and profit sustainability in Alibaba E-commerce Group,” Chief Financial Officer Toby Xu said.

Excluding investment gains and other items, non-GAAP net income leapt 92% to 19.9 billion yuan (S$3.85 billion), helped by stronger profitability and narrowing losses in its quick-commerce business.

Alibaba’s shares are down about 40% this year, as investors worry about weak consumer demand in China and rising spending on AI and cloud infrastructure.

Free cash flow was an outflow of 34.47 billion yuan in the quarter, compared with an outflow of 21.84 billion yuan a year earlier. Alibaba said the increase reflected higher spending on cloud infrastructure, partly offset by lower losses at Taobao Instant Commerce and higher customer pre-payments for cloud services.

Capital expenditure rose 60% to 50.48 billion yuan.

Alibaba reported quarterly revenue of 271.52 billion yuan, ahead of analysts’ average estimate of 269.81 billion yuan, according to LSEG data.

AI cloud and computing services revenue totalled 60.97 billion yuan. Alibaba has sharply increased spending on AI infrastructure, proprietary models and applications, betting on the technology as a key growth driver.

Adjusted earnings per American Depositary Share were 8.10 yuan, below analysts’ expectations of 11.16 yuan.

In September, Alibaba unveiled plans to expand global data-centre capacity to more than 20 gigawatts by 2032 and said its next-generation Qwen 4 model was in training. Its chip-design unit T-Head, which confidentially filed for a Hong Kong listing earlier in November, also unveiled a new AI processor scheduled for commercial release in early 2027.

Alibaba launched a US$10 billion (S$12.92 billion) share placement in August, saying the proceeds would fund computing infrastructure and AI data centres.

The company recently reorganised its businesses into four main units: e-commerce, AI cloud and computing services, AI model applications and other businesses. REUTERS
